meta.title: Who really said "It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Lee Iacocca, on the day Chrysler went into Chapter 11 — 30 April 2009. A written statement issued to Newsweek, not an interview remark.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes'?
meta.ogDescription: Lee Iacocca, who had rescued Chrysler thirty years earlier. The rest of the statement is an argument, and it usually gets cut.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1924–2019 · Ford and Chrysler executive; Chrysler chairman and CEO 1979–1992
answer.sourceLine: It is the second sentence of a statement Iacocca issued on 30 April 2009, the day the Obama administration announced that Chrysler would file for Chapter 11 — thirty years after Iacocca had talked Washington into the loan guarantees that saved the same company. Newsweek published it ↗ the same day, in a piece by Julie Halpert, and is careful about the form: Iacocca “issued the following statement”. He wrote it; he did not say it in an interview.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: 30 April 2009 — the day Chrysler’s Chapter 11 filing was announced
“It Pains Me”: Lee Iacocca on Chrysler’s slide into bankruptcy, Newsweek Web Exclusive
A written statement, quoted in full — not an interview answer

source.excerpt: This is a sad day for me. It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes. But Chrysler has been in trouble before, and we got through it, and I believe they can do it again. If they’re smart, they’ll bring together a consortium of workers, plant managers and dealers to come up with real solutions. These are the folks on the front lines, and they’re the key to survival. Let’s face it, if your car breaks down, you’re not going to take it to the White House to get fixed. But, if your company breaks down, you’ve got to go to the experts on the ground, not the bureaucrats.
trail: We read the source. “It Pains Me”: Lee Iacocca on Chrysler’s slide into bankruptcy ↗, by Julie Halpert, Newsweek Web Exclusive, dated 30 April 2009, captured by the Internet Archive on 4 May 2009. It introduces the quotation with “Iacocca took time to reflect on the demise of the company he once led and rescued and issued the following statement”, then prints it whole.
The sentence is verbatim in that statement: “This is a sad day for me. It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes.”
Wikiquote’s sourced Lee Iacocca page ↗ carries the same quotation and cites the same Halpert article, giving the date as 30 April 2009.

The framing matters and the article supplies it: Halpert notes that the last time Chrysler faced bankruptcy was in 1979, when Iacocca — one year into his tenure as CEO — “convinced the government to bail out the company and provide $1.5 billion in federally backed loans”, and that the loans were repaid early. Wikipedia ↗ dates his Chrysler chairmanship and CEO tenure to 20 September 1979 – 31 December 1992.
“My old company” is Chrysler, not Ford. The statement names Chrysler in its next sentence, and Halpert’s article is about Chrysler’s filing throughout.
source.excerptNote: The statement runs on: “Every day I talk to dealers and managers, who are passionate and full of ideas. No one wants Chrysler to survive more than they do. So I’d say to the Obama administration, don’t leave them out. Put their passion and ideas to work.” Read in full from Newsweek’s page of 30 April 2009 ↗. The famous sentence is the setup; the point of the statement is the request that follows it.

author.name: Lee Iacocca
author.heading: About Lee Iacocca
author.metaLine: 1924–2019 · Ford and Chrysler executive; Chrysler chairman and CEO 1979–1992
author.bio: Lido Anthony “Lee” Iacocca (15 October 1924 – 2 July 2019) was born in Allentown, Pennsylvania, made his name at Ford with the Mustang, rose to its presidency and was fired in 1978. He moved to Chrysler, won federal loan guarantees that kept it alive, and built the company back on the K-car and the minivan before retiring at the end of 1992. He was his own pitchman on television and one of the few industrialists Americans could name. He founded the Iacocca Foundation for type 1 diabetes research after his wife Mary died of complications of the disease.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not in doubt — this is Iacocca’s own sentence, dated and sourced. Two things about it do get mangled in reuse.

items.why: Newsweek is precise about this: Iacocca “issued the following statement”. It is not a remark from a sit-down interview, and a page quoting it as speech is quoting it wrongly. See the article ↗.

Cut at “on the ropes”, the sentence reads as an elegy. In the statement it is the opening of an argument: bring in “a consortium of workers, plant managers and dealers”, because “if your company breaks down, you’ve got to go to the experts on the ground, not the bureaucrats.” Iacocca was lobbying, not mourning.

Iacocca is equally famous for the Mustang, so “my old company” can read as Ford. It is Chrysler: the next sentence of the statement names it, and the whole article is about Chrysler’s Chapter 11 filing.

misattribution.truthLine: Lee Iacocca wrote it, on 30 April 2009, about Chrysler, in a statement issued to Newsweek — read the original ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In 1979 Iacocca had argued Washington into $1.5 billion in federally backed loans, then built the company back with the K-car and the minivan and repaid the money early. It made him the most famous businessman in America and the standing proof that a government rescue could work.

Thirty years later the same company was filing for Chapter 11 and he was eighty-four and had no part in it. That is what gives the sentence its weight: the man who wrote the playbook, watching from outside while someone else ran the same play.
detailsBody: Halpert’s article makes the contrast explicit: “on Thursday, as President Obama announced the plan for Chrysler to file Chapter 11 bankruptcy, there is no white knight like Iacocca to save the company.” She attributes the collapse to Chrysler’s reliance on minivans and sport-utility vehicles and its neglect of fuel-efficient cars — which is to say, to the commercial logic of the vehicles Iacocca himself had introduced.

The advice in the statement is the part worth reading twice, because it is a specific procedural objection rather than sentiment: consult the dealers, plant managers and workers instead of the administration’s task force. “Let’s face it, if your car breaks down, you’re not going to take it to the White House to get fixed.” Coming from the man whose rescue depended entirely on Washington, it is a more complicated remark than it first sounds.
context.pull: The man who wrote the playbook for rescuing Chrysler, watching from outside while someone else ran the same play.

sourcesVerified.claim: Newsweek's Web Exclusive of 30 April 2009 by Julie Halpert, headlined "'It Pains Me': Lee Iacocca on Chrysler's slide into bankruptcy", prints Iacocca's statement containing verbatim: 'This is a sad day for me. It pains me to see my old company, which has meant so much to America, on the ropes. But Chrysler has been in trouble before, and we got through it, and I believe they can do it again.'

The same article introduces the quotation with 'Iacocca took time to reflect on the demise of the company he once led and rescued and issued the following statement' - establishing that it was a written statement rather than an interview answer.

The same article continues the statement: 'If they're smart, they'll bring together a consortium of workers, plant managers and dealers to come up with real solutions... Let's face it, if your car breaks down, you're not going to take it to the White House to get fixed. But, if your company breaks down, you've got to go to the experts on the ground, not the bureaucrats.'

The same article states that the last time Chrysler faced bankruptcy was in 1979, when Iacocca 'convinced the government to bail out the company and provide $1.5 billion in federally backed loans', that he retired from Chrysler in 1992, and that 'on Thursday, as President Obama announced the plan for Chrysler to file Chapter 11 bankruptcy, there is no white knight like Iacocca to save the company.'
Wikiquote's Lee Iacocca page carries this quotation and cites Julie Halpert, 'It Pains Me', Newsweek, April 30, 2009.

Wikipedia gives Lido Anthony 'Lee' Iacocca's dates as October 15, 1924 - July 2, 2019, Ford president and CEO December 1970 - July 1978, and Chrysler chairman and CEO September 20, 1979 - December 31, 1992.
